def: The basic building block of agentic systems: a single model call enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory, where the model itself writes its search queries, picks which tool to call and decides what to retain.
eg: Start here. Many business problems need nothing more than one well-augmented call, and every step up in complexity has to earn its extra latency, cost and unpredictability.

def: A system in which models and tools are orchestrated through code paths the developer wrote in advance, so the order of steps is fixed and predictable even though individual steps call an LLM.
eg: Choose it when the task is well defined and repeatable or when auditors need a deterministic order. The contrast with an agent is who decides the next step: your code or the model.

def: A system in which the model itself directs its process, choosing each next step and tool call and looping on feedback from the environment until the task is finished or a stopping condition fires. It suits open-ended problems whose path cannot be hard-coded.
eg: Autonomy buys flexibility at the price of cost, latency and compounding errors, so it needs sandboxes, limits and checks. If you could draw the steps in advance, a fixed pipeline is usually the better choice.

def: A pattern that splits a task into a fixed sequence of model calls, each consuming the output of the previous one, with optional programmatic checks between steps. It trades extra latency for higher accuracy because every call is an easier job.
eg: Typical use: draft an outline, check it against criteria in code, then write the document. The checks between steps are called gates.

def: A pattern that first classifies an input and then sends it to a specialized prompt, tool set or model, so tuning for one kind of request does not hurt another. Common questions can go to a small, cheap model and unusual ones to a stronger model.
eg: Works when categories are distinct and classification is accurate. It is the usual first answer to a mixed workload with very different cost and quality needs.

def: A pattern that runs model calls at the same time and combines the results in code, either by splitting a task into independent parts or by running the same task several times for diverse attempts and a vote.
eg: Sectioning buys speed and focus (a screening call running beside the main call is a classic case); voting buys confidence. Neither involves the model deciding the split.

def: A pattern where a central model call breaks a task into subtasks that could not be predicted in advance, delegates them to worker calls and synthesizes the results. It looks like parallel fan-out, but the subtasks are decided at run time from the input.
eg: Fits changes whose scope depends on the input, such as edits across an unknown number of files. The difference from sectioning is that the split is not pre-defined.

def: A pattern in which one model call produces a draft and another critiques it against clear criteria, looping until the output is good enough. It works when feedback measurably improves the result and a model can supply that feedback.
eg: Good for nuanced translation or multi-round search. Without crisp criteria the loop adds cost without adding quality.

def: The design rule to begin with one optimized model call, add retrieval or examples next, and introduce workflows or autonomous loops only when measurements show the simpler option falls short, because added autonomy costs latency, tokens and predictability.
eg: Frequently the right answer to over-engineered proposals. Complexity is justified by evaluation evidence, not by how impressive the architecture looks.

def: On the Messages API, the cycle in which your code sends a request with tools, the model answers with stop reason tool_use, your code runs the requested tools and returns tool_result blocks, and the cycle repeats until the model ends its turn.
eg: The model never executes your tools itself. Loops should also exit on stop reasons such as max_tokens and refusal, and be capped by turns or spend.

def: A check made before choosing an architecture: whether the business problem has language-shaped inputs, tolerates probabilistic output, offers a way to verify results and can absorb the cost of an error, rather than reaching for an LLM design because it is available.
eg: This is architecture practice rather than a Claude feature. It is the first step in translating a business problem into a solution and it often points to the simplest pattern.

def: The path that carries signals from outputs back into a system, such as user corrections, evaluator verdicts and tool results, so prompts, retrieval data and routing rules can be improved. A complete design names its inputs, processing, outputs and this return path.
eg: Architectures that stop at 'output' cannot improve. Corrections captured from reviewers also become the evaluation set for the next change.

def: The framing used to tie a Claude solution to outcomes the business cares about: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost and performance against service levels. Each architecture decision should be defensible against at least one of them.
eg: Architects use it to justify trade-offs to sponsors: caching and routing serve cost, streaming and effort tuning serve performance, automation of manual steps serves efficiency.

def: The unit used to compare models and designs: total spend divided by tasks actually solved. A pricier model that needs fewer turns can be cheaper per success than a cheaper one, and a changed tokenizer can distort per-token comparisons.
eg: Anthropic's cost guidance compares on this basis. Quote it instead of price per million tokens when defending a model choice.

def: The end-to-end time a request is allowed to take, divided among retrieval, model generation, tool calls and post-processing, so each design choice (model size, effort, streaming, caching, parallel calls) can be checked against the user-facing target.
eg: Build it before choosing components. A budget makes it obvious that a slow retrieval step cannot be fixed by a faster model.

def: A checkpoint in an automated flow where a person, or a stricter policy, must confirm before an irreversible or high-impact action such as a refund, a deletion or an external message proceeds. It is placed by blast radius and reversibility, not applied to every step.
eg: Gating everything defeats automation; gating nothing and relying on prompt wording is the opposite failure. Read-only and easily undone steps usually run freely.

def: The failure mode in which a mistake early in a long autonomous run feeds every later step, so small per-step error rates multiply across many steps. It is reduced with checkpoints, verification, resumable state and stopping conditions.
eg: Agents are stateful and long running. Restarting from scratch after each failure is expensive, so durable state and resumption are part of the design.

def: Choosing between writing your own agent loop and runtime on the Messages API, embedding the Agent SDK in a process you operate, or using a hosted harness such as Managed Agents. It is driven by the control you need, the operational burden you accept and the data-handling terms you must meet.
eg: Phrase it as practice, not product trivia: more control means more to build, secure and run. Hosted options cost control and have their own data-retention terms.

def: Anthropic's hosted agent harness, currently in beta, that runs the agent loop, tools and a sandbox for you: you define an agent, an environment and sessions, then exchange events and stream results. It is built for long-running, asynchronous work with minimal infrastructure.
eg: It is stateful by design and, at the time of writing, is not eligible for zero data retention or HIPAA BAA coverage, which matters when the data rules decide the platform.

def: A Python and TypeScript library that embeds the agent loop, built-in tools, permissions, hooks, subagents and sessions that power Claude Code inside an application process you operate yourself.
eg: It spawns a CLI subprocess per session, so hosting it means managing long-lived processes and local state, unlike a stateless API wrapper.

def: Direct prompting access to the model, where your code owns the agent loop, tool execution and state. It offers the finest control and is the base layer beneath the other options.
eg: Choose it for custom loops and fine-grained control. The SDK's tool runner can drive the loop but does not change who operates it.

def: The configuration of where sessions run: an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox with a chosen package set and network policy, or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure. Every session receives its own isolated container from it.
eg: Set the network policy explicitly: limiting hosts to those the agent needs is the recommended default, and omitting it may leave networking unrestricted.

def: A running agent instance inside an environment, performing one task. Conversation history, sandbox state and outputs persist server-side, and the session can be steered, interrupted, resumed and capped with a budget.
eg: Sessions are the unit you monitor, bill and delete. History stays until the session is deleted, which matters for retention decisions.

def: A hard dollar ceiling set when a Managed Agents session is created and priced at list rates. When it is reached the session pauses with stop reason budget_reached instead of quietly running up cost, and raising the budget resumes it.
eg: The textbook example of programmatic enforcement: a platform limit holds, whereas a prompt asking the agent to be frugal does not.

def: A limit placed on an autonomous loop, such as a maximum number of turns or a maximum spend, so a confused or runaway run stops with an explicit error result instead of continuing indefinitely.
eg: In the Agent SDK these are max_turns and max_budget_usd. Spend can overshoot by the cost of the response that crossed the cap, so leave headroom.

def: What happens when one subtask fills an agent's window with bulky output that is irrelevant to later subtasks, diluting attention and degrading its reasoning. It is one of three situations in which splitting work across agents pays off.
eg: The other two are independent work that can run in parallel and specialization of tools or instructions. Outside those, coordination cost usually exceeds the benefit.

def: A property of delegated agents: each works in its own separate conversation, keeps its intermediate tool calls and results there, and returns only a condensed final message to its parent.
eg: The parent receives a summary of perhaps a thousand or two tokens instead of everything the helper read, which keeps the lead agent focused.

def: Dividing work along context boundaries so each agent keeps all the information its piece needs, for example the agent that builds a feature also writes its tests. The split is made only where context can truly be separated.
eg: Good boundaries: independent research paths, components behind clean interfaces and black-box verification. Bad boundaries: sequential phases of the same work.

def: Splitting work by type of activity, such as planner, implementer, tester and reviewer, which forces constant hand-offs in which each recipient lacks the reasoning behind earlier steps. Teams doing this often spend more tokens coordinating than working.
eg: Anthropic calls the information loss a telephone game. It is usually the wrong decomposition even though it mirrors how human teams are organized.

def: A dedicated agent whose only job is to test or validate another agent's output against explicit success criteria, using tools such as a test runner. It needs little context from the builder, so it avoids the hand-off losses of other splits.
eg: Useful for quality checks, compliance checking and output validation, and when the orchestrator is weaker or verification needs specialized tools.

def: A separate agent instance spawned by a main agent for a focused piece of work. Its context starts fresh, holding only the task prompt it is handed, it can have its own instructions, tools and model, and it hands back just its final message.
eg: Classic trap: it does not inherit the parent's conversation, so the delegation prompt must carry file paths, constraints and decisions.

def: In Claude Managed Agents, a program the agent writes at run time that runs many agents in phases in the background and combines their results, leaving the main thread free to talk to the user. The agent cannot send follow-up messages to a run's threads afterwards.
eg: Contrast with delegated helpers whose threads persist for follow-ups. Every agent in a run uses tokens, so pair it with a session budget.

def: A multi-model pattern in which a faster, cheaper model does the work and can consult a higher-intelligence model mid-task for a plan or course correction. It only helps if the working model actually consults, so the consult rate has to be measured.
eg: The advisor tool definition adds about a thousand prompt tokens even when never used. Compare against the same model at higher effort before adopting it.

def: A cost pattern in which a stronger model plans and splits the work while lower-cost workers handle bulk subtasks, each in its own context. Measured savings appeared for routine work with a long cost tail and for work larger than one context window.
eg: For a single dependent chain, or work that fits in one window, the stronger model alone at lower effort came out ahead in Anthropic's measurements.

def: The extra spend of multi-agent designs, commonly several times that of one agent (3 to 10 times in Anthropic's testing, and about 15 times a chat in its research system), caused by duplicated context, coordination messages and result summaries.
eg: It is why multi-agent systems need tasks valuable enough to pay for the extra thoroughness. The main benefit is coverage, not speed.

term: Claude model tiers (Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku)
def: The four current capability levels, from highest capability and price to lowest: Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, Opus 5.5 for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, Sonnet 5.5 for the best balance of speed and intelligence, and Haiku 5.5 for the lowest latency and price.
eg: Pick by measuring on your own task, not by reputation. Start efficiency-first with the small tier or capability-first with the strong one, then adjust using evaluations.

def: The smallest, fastest and lowest-priced current model, positioned for high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, extraction and routing, and for sub-agent tasks. A sensible first model to try when outputs are easy to check.
eg: Upgrade only when evaluations show a capability gap. Its default effort is medium.

def: The mid-tier current model offering the best combination of speed and intelligence for everyday coding, data analysis, content creation and agentic tool use across enterprise workloads.
eg: A common production workhorse. Compare it against the tier above at lower effort before paying for more.

def: The current model Anthropic suggests starting with for most workloads. It is built for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, with adaptive thinking always on and medium as its default effort.
eg: It supports fast mode, now without a beta header or access request. Its prompt-cache reads are discounted more steeply than most earlier models.

def: Anthropic's most capable model open to all customers, aimed at demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, or at cases where evaluations on the next tier down at higher effort still fall short. It is priced above the other tiers.
eg: Reach for it last, after trying effort changes on a cheaper tier. A sibling with the same capabilities is limited to organizations verified through Anthropic programs.

def: A request setting (output_config.effort) that trades thoroughness for speed and cost within one model by governing how much thinking, tool calling and self-checking it does, from low through medium, high and xhigh to max. It is often a better lever than switching models.
eg: Defaults differ by model, so set it explicitly and run a sweep on your own evaluations. Changing the top-level value mid-conversation invalidates cached messages.

def: A thinking mode in which the model decides for itself whether and how much to reason before answering, steered by the effort level and the difficulty of the request. On the newest models, manual thinking token budgets are rejected with an error.
eg: Thinking tokens are billed as output and count toward max_tokens, so leave room. Hand-written reasoning scaffolds are largely replaced by it.

def: An option on selected Opus models, open on Opus 5.5 without an access request, that raises output speed, by up to about 2.5 times, at premium pricing. It lowers generation latency without changing which model answers.
eg: Switching speed settings invalidates cached system and message prefixes, and it is not available inside batches.

def: A model identifier that always refers to the same snapshot, so behavior does not shift under production traffic. Current Claude IDs are pinned, and moving to a newer model is a deliberate change that should be tested first.
eg: Retirement dates are published per model. Plan upgrades with a prompt audit and an evaluation run instead of waiting for a deadline.

def: The total tokens a model can consider in one request: the system prompt, tool definitions, every message and tool result, and the output it generates including thinking. The current Claude models offer one million tokens, but more is not automatically better.
eg: Cached tokens still occupy it, because caching changes what you pay, not whether the tokens count.

def: The decline in recall and accuracy as the number of tokens in the window grows, so curating what is in context matters as much as how much fits.
eg: The reason a big window does not remove the need for retrieval, clearing, compaction or delegation.

def: The discipline of curating the smallest set of high-signal tokens in the window at every inference step, covering the system prompt, tools, examples, retrieved data and message history, as the natural extension of writing individual prompts.
eg: Prompt engineering writes instructions; this manages the whole state the model sees, repeatedly, as an agent loops.

def: A feature that reuses the processed prefix of a prompt (tools, then system, then messages) across requests, so repeat tokens are billed at a fraction of the input price and processed faster, after a one-time write premium.
eg: Put stable content first and volatile content last. It works on all active models and on the main cloud platforms.

def: A cache_control marker on a content block telling the API to cache everything up to and including that block. Up to four can be used, and each should sit at the end of the last block that is identical across requests.
eg: A breakpoint on a block that changes every request, such as one holding a timestamp, writes a new entry each time and never reads one.

def: How long a cached prefix survives without being reused: five minutes by default, refreshed at no charge on each hit, or one hour at a higher write price for workloads with long pauses between requests.
eg: Choose by the gaps between requests. Seconds apart means the default, and frequent pauses of several minutes favor the one-hour option.

term: Cache write premium and read discount
def: The pricing shape of caching: writing a prefix costs more than normal input (1.25 times for the five-minute lifetime, 2 times for one hour), while reading it costs a small fraction, generally a tenth and less on some models. A write pays for itself after about one reuse.
eg: Misses are costly: a broken prefix re-pays the write price for the whole prefix instead of the read price.

def: What happens when anything earlier in the prefix changes: matching is exact and cumulative in the order tools, system, messages, so editing tool definitions, the system prompt, or thinking and effort settings can force everything after the change to be rewritten.
eg: Put per-request text after the last breakpoint and make unavoidable changes at natural breaks, such as the first request after a compaction.

def: A beta feature in which the API replaces the older turns of a long conversation with a summary the model writes on the server, so work can continue past the window limit without custom summarization code.
eg: Choose between on-demand and threshold-triggered modes. Overly aggressive summaries can drop details whose importance only appears later.

def: A server-side technique that clears chosen content, such as old tool results or earlier thinking blocks, once the conversation passes a threshold, leaving placeholders. The client keeps its full history untouched.
eg: Clearing breaks the cached prefix, so clear a meaningful amount at a time. It is a lighter touch than summarizing everything.

def: A client-side tool through which Claude reads and writes files under a /memories path that your application maps to storage you control, letting an agent keep notes and state across sessions without holding them in the window.
eg: Because your code executes the operations, you must also guard against path traversal and decide per-user storage and retention.

def: The top-level instructions that set a model's role, rules, tone, output format and background for a whole conversation, kept apart from per-turn user content. Its stable text also forms part of the cacheable prefix.
eg: Aim for the right altitude: specific enough to steer, flexible enough to give the model heuristics instead of brittle if-else logic.

def: Asking the model to perform a task from instructions alone, with no worked examples. A sensible default for capable models, upgraded to examples when format or judgment turns out inconsistent.
eg: Test it first. Adding examples you did not need only adds tokens.

def: Including a handful of relevant, diverse and clearly delimited examples (three to five works well) in the prompt to steer format, tone and judgment more reliably than description alone.
eg: Curate canonical examples instead of listing every edge case, and wrap them in tags so they cannot be mistaken for instructions.

def: Encouraging step-by-step reasoning before the final answer. On current models built-in adaptive thinking at a suitable effort replaces hand-written reasoning scaffolds, and prompts that ask for reasoning to be written out can be declined.
eg: Manual versions remain a fallback only for models with thinking off. Do not ask for reasoning fields in outputs or tool inputs.

def: Wrapping each kind of content in descriptive tags such as instructions, context, document and example so the model can tell directions, data and samples apart. It reduces misreading in long prompts that mix them.
eg: Use consistent tag names and nest them when content has hierarchy. Exact formatting matters less as models improve, but separation still helps.

def: Placing long documents near the top of the prompt, above the question and instructions, with each document wrapped in tags, and the query last. Asking the model to quote relevant passages first helps it focus.
eg: Anthropic reports queries at the end improving response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with multi-document inputs.

def: A reusable prompt skeleton with fixed instructions and named slots filled at run time, ideally assembled from separately maintained modules so the stable parts form a cacheable prefix and the variable parts come last.
eg: Treat it as practice: modules make prompts reviewable and reusable, and ordering them static-first is what lets caching work.

def: Filesystem-based packages of instructions, scripts and resources, led by a SKILL.md with a name and description, that Claude loads on demand so specialist expertise is available without occupying context until a task needs it.
eg: Only the name and description are always loaded, about a hundred tokens per skill. They are not available on every cloud platform.

def: An endpoint that returns how many input tokens a prospective request would use, including tools, system prompt, images and documents, so you can budget, route or truncate before sending.
eg: Use it to avoid 'prompt too long' failures and to size cache prefixes. It estimates input only.

def: Features that constrain generation to a JSON Schema, through output_config.format for responses and strict: true for tool inputs, guaranteeing parseable, correctly typed results without retries.
eg: Reach for them when a downstream system rejects schema violations. Availability differs by cloud platform, so check before committing.

def: A hard limit on the tokens in one response, covering thinking and visible text. The model cannot see it, so lowering it does not make answers shorter, and hitting it ends the turn with stop reason max_tokens.
eg: Treat max_tokens stops as failures. To save money, ask for shorter answers in the prompt or use effort, which the model can see.

def: A message with the system role appended to the messages array to change instructions partway through a conversation without editing the top-level system field, so the cached prefix stays intact. It is supported on recent models only.
eg: The alternative, rewriting the top-level system prompt, invalidates the cache from that point on.

def: Controls implemented in code or configuration, such as removed tools, permission rules, hooks, schemas and server-side validation, that hold whatever the model says. Used where consequences are severe, whereas prompt wording only guides probabilistic behavior.
eg: A recurring exam principle: do not rely on 'never do X' in a prompt when a limit can be enforced in the tool or back end.

def: Reviewing prompts against the model currently in use to remove text written for an older one, such as 'verify twice', hand-made reasoning scaffolds or contradictory rules, which newer models obey literally, adding cost or hurting accuracy.
eg: A free win on every model change. Anthropic's measurements showed old prompts costing more per ticket on a newer model with no accuracy gain until audited.

def: A configuration problem in which an agent holds more tools, permissions or instructions than its task needs, inflating context, blurring tool selection and widening the blast radius of mistakes or attacks. The fix is to remove, scope or defer what is not needed.
eg: Symptoms: wrong-tool calls between look-alike tools, large baseline token counts and a role that can do things it never should.

def: Giving an agent only the tools and scopes its role needs and removing the rest from its configuration, instead of keeping them and adding logging or confirmation prompts. Removal eliminates the exposure, while monitoring only detects misuse after the fact.
eg: Logging and confirmations are compensating controls. When a role never needs a capability, delete it from the configuration.

def: Disabling every tool of a connected MCP server by default and enabling only the named ones, using enabled: false in the toolset's default configuration plus per-tool overrides. It also protects against tools the server adds later.
eg: A denylist leaves everything else switched on, including future additions, so an allowlist is the safer pattern for sensitive assistants.

def: The detailed plain-text explanation attached to a tool that says what it does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means and what it does not return. It is the single biggest factor in whether the model picks and uses the tool correctly.
eg: Write several sentences, not a label. Vague one-liners cause wrong calls between look-alike tools and are worth fixing before adding examples.

def: Grouping related operations into fewer, more capable tools with an action parameter, and prefixing names by service, such as github_list_prs, to cut selection ambiguity as the tool library grows.
eg: If a human engineer cannot say which tool applies in a situation, the model cannot be expected to do better.

def: A server-side tool that lets the model search a catalog by regex or BM25 and load only the matching definitions on demand, instead of sending every schema up front. It returns up to five matches by default and can cut definition tokens by over 85 percent in large setups.
eg: Pairs with defer_loading. It adds a lookup turn, trading a little latency for a much smaller baseline context and better selection.

def: A flag, defer_loading, on a tool or MCP toolset that withholds its definition from the initial context until a search discovers it. It keeps the baseline prompt small and cache-friendly, and at least one tool, normally the search tool, must stay loaded.
eg: On an MCP toolset, setting it in default_config defers every tool of that server at once.

def: Letting the model write code that calls your tools inside the code execution sandbox, so loops, filters and joins run there and only the final result returns to the context. It cuts round trips and tokens for multi-tool chains.
eg: Needs the code execution tool and an allowed_callers setting on each tool. It is not eligible for zero data retention and is not offered on Bedrock or Google Cloud.

def: An open protocol through which a host application's clients connect to servers that expose tools, resources and prompts, so one integration works across many AI applications instead of a custom connector for every pairing.
eg: Choose it when several clients or agents must share an integration with consistent authentication. For a single known system, a direct call is often simpler.

def: The three roles in the protocol: the host application coordinates and enforces policy, each client it creates keeps a one-to-one connection with a single server, and servers expose capabilities. Servers should not see the whole conversation or each other.
eg: The host owns consent and security boundaries, which is why untrusted server metadata must never be given more authority than the host decides.

def: The three server building blocks and who controls each: tools are model-controlled actions, resources are application-controlled context data, and prompts are user-controlled templates such as slash commands.
eg: A frequent trap is mixing up who triggers each. The Messages API connector supports only the tool primitive.

def: The standard transport for remote MCP servers: each message is an HTTP POST to a single endpoint, and replies arrive as a JSON body or a request-scoped event stream. It replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport, which is deprecated.
eg: Pick it for shared, centrally hosted servers that need OAuth. A broken stream loses the in-flight request, which the client must re-issue.

def: The transport in which the client launches the server as a local subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited messages over standard input and output. It suits local tools, and credentials come from the environment instead of OAuth.
eg: The Messages API connector cannot reach a local stdio server directly, because it needs a publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint.

def: The design of the 2026-07-28 protocol revision: the initialize handshake and protocol-level sessions are gone, every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities, and servers advertise theirs through a discovery call. Cross-call state uses explicit handles passed as ordinary tool arguments.
eg: Makes servers easier to scale behind ordinary load balancers, because no request depends on a connection-bound session.

def: The MCP pattern for a server that needs more input mid-request: it returns an input_required result describing what it needs (sampling, elicitation or roots), and the client retries the original request with the answers. No server-held state or sticky routing is required.
eg: Replaced server-initiated requests in the 2026-07-28 revision, which is a breaking change for servers written against older versions.

def: Optional transport-level authorization for HTTP-based servers: the server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server and advertises its authorization server through protected resource metadata, and clients use PKCE and the resource parameter. Local stdio servers take credentials from the environment instead.
eg: Scope guidance arrives in the WWW-Authenticate challenge, and clients ask for the least scope that works, stepping up when needed.

def: Requiring that an access token be issued for, and accepted only by, the specific resource server it names, using the resource indicator and the audience claim, so a token minted for one service cannot be replayed at another.
eg: MCP servers must reject tokens not meant for them. It is the control that closes confused-deputy and passthrough holes.

def: The forbidden anti-pattern in which an MCP server forwards the access token it received from its client to an upstream API. The server must instead act as its own OAuth client and obtain a separate token for upstream calls.
eg: The giveaway in a scenario: a downstream service accepts a token that was never issued for it, so audit trails and scopes are meaningless.

def: A flaw in which a privileged intermediary, such as an MCP proxy using a static client ID, is tricked into acting with its own authority on behalf of an attacker. Mitigations include per-client user consent, exact redirect URI matching and audience checks.
eg: The pattern generalizes: whenever a service holds more authority than its caller, make it check the caller's authority, not just its own.

def: A beta Messages API feature that lets the API itself connect to remote MCP servers over HTTPS, through mcp_servers and mcp_toolset entries and an optional OAuth bearer token, with no MCP client of your own. It supports tool calls only.
eg: Not eligible for zero data retention, and not offered on Bedrock or Google Cloud. You obtain and refresh the OAuth token yourself.

def: Calling a system's own REST API or command-line tool from your code or an agent's shell instead of through MCP. It is the simplest and most predictable choice for one known system or a deterministic step.
eg: A protocol earns its place when many clients or agents must share an integration, not when one service calls one API.

def: A design in which one agent hands work to another agent that has its own model, instructions, tools and context, instead of exposing a system as a function. It fits counterparts that need autonomy, such as delegated helpers, workflow runs or a peer team's agent.
eg: This is architecture practice; the Anthropic docs describe it through subagents, workflow runs and advisors rather than one named protocol.

def: A static secret generated in the Claude Console and sent as a bearer token. Personal keys act as one user and service-account keys as a non-human identity; both suit development and servers with sound secret storage, and legacy workspace keys are discouraged.
eg: Never ship one in browser or mobile code. For production on a platform with its own identity, prefer federation.

def: A named non-human identity inside an organization that owns keys or federated tokens for shared and automated workloads, so access survives staff changes and can be audited per workload.
eg: It has no email, password or console login, and it becomes active in a workspace when added as a member.

def: A mechanism that exchanges a short-lived OIDC identity token from your own provider (cloud IAM, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions and others) for a short-lived Claude token bound to a service account, so no static key is stored. An issuer, a service account and a rule must be configured first.
eg: Only as strong as the upstream identity provider. Token lifetime is configurable from one minute to a day.

def: A workspace-scoped collection of credentials for third-party services belonging to one end user, referenced by ID when a session is created, so secrets stay out of agent definitions and each run acts with the right person's access.
eg: Vaults are workspace-scoped: any key with access to the workspace can reference them, so scope workspaces carefully.

def: A per-toolset setting that decides whether a server-executed tool runs automatically, waits for human approval or has each call judged by the server: always_allow, always_ask or auto. The agent toolset defaults to allow and MCP toolsets default to ask.
eg: A policy controls when an enabled tool runs. To remove a tool entirely, disable it instead.

def: The AWS-operated way to use Claude: the Messages API shape served from AWS-managed infrastructure inside the AWS security boundary, with IAM authentication, AWS billing and no Anthropic operator access to inference. Features follow AWS's release schedule.
eg: The choice when AWS must be the sole data processor or when FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 or HIPAA-ready environments are required.

def: Anthropic's own platform, with the full Claude API surface and typically same-day features, reached through an AWS account: AWS supplies identity (SigV4 or a key), IAM scoping and Marketplace billing, while Anthropic operates inference and is the data processor.
eg: Choose it for newest features such as Skills, the MCP connector and Managed Agents with AWS procurement, if Anthropic may be the processor.

def: Claude served through Google Cloud's Agent Platform, where the model is named in the endpoint URL and anthropic_version, set to vertex-2023-10-16, goes in the request body. Global, multi-region and regional endpoints trade availability against residency.
eg: Code execution, Skills, the MCP connector and Message Batches are not offered there, so plan client-side equivalents.

def: Claude behind Azure-native endpoints in a Foundry resource, authenticated by API key or Microsoft Entra ID and billed through the Azure Marketplace. The deployment name you create is the value passed as the model, and a deployment can be hosted on Azure or on Anthropic.
eg: Some features, such as Skills, code execution and the Files API, require the hosted-on-Anthropic option and return errors on Azure-hosted deployments.

def: On Bedrock and Google Cloud, a global endpoint routes dynamically across regions for maximum availability at the base price, while regional (or multi-region) endpoints pin processing to a geography for residency at roughly a 10 percent premium.
eg: Residency requirements push you to regional; availability and price favor global. Provisioned throughput on Google Cloud requires regional.

def: Retrieving relevant passages from a knowledge base at question time and adding them to the prompt, so answers are grounded in current, private data. Result quality depends on chunking, indexing and retrieval at least as much as on the model.
eg: When answers are confidently wrong after a data change, look at retrieval and indexing first. A corpus that fits comfortably in a cached prompt may not need RAG at all.

def: Splitting documents into retrievable pieces, usually a few hundred tokens, where size, boundaries and overlap shape recall: pieces that are too small lose context, and pieces that are too large dilute relevance and waste tokens.
eg: Prefer structure-aware boundaries such as sections or clauses, and carry headings or document metadata with each piece.

def: A model that turns text into vectors so semantically similar passages sit close together. Anthropic does not offer one, and its documentation points to providers such as Voyage AI; choose by domain fit, latency, cost and customization.
eg: A common false statement is that Claude produces the embeddings. Claude consumes the retrieved text; another model creates the vectors.

def: Retrieval by nearest-neighbor similarity between a query embedding and chunk embeddings. It is strong on paraphrase and meaning but can miss exact identifiers such as error codes or part numbers.
eg: Pair it with lexical search whenever users search by identifiers, names or quoted phrases.

def: A ranking function based on exact term matching with document-length normalization, effective for rare tokens such as error codes, names and part numbers where embeddings blur. It is usually combined with vector search.
eg: It builds on TF-IDF. Unique identifiers are its sweet spot.

def: Running vector and lexical retrieval together, then merging and de-duplicating the two ranked lists with a rank-fusion method, so both meaning and exact matches contribute to the final candidates.
eg: In Anthropic's tests, embeddings plus BM25 beat embeddings alone.

def: An indexing technique in which a model writes a short chunk-specific context note, typically 50 to 100 tokens, that is prepended to each chunk before embedding and before building the lexical index. In Anthropic's tests it cut failed retrievals by 49 percent, and by 67 percent with reranking.
eg: Prompt caching of the source document keeps the one-time indexing cost low. It fixes chunks that say 'the company' without naming which one.

def: A second-stage step that rescores a wide candidate list against the query with a dedicated model and keeps only the best few chunks for the prompt, improving precision and trimming tokens at the cost of a little latency.
eg: Anthropic's test retrieved 150 candidates and passed the top 20 to the model. More candidates reranked means more latency.

def: Document blocks with citations enabled, and search result blocks that carry a source and title, let Claude attribute each claim to the passage that supports it, with the source identifier you supplied, so answers can be verified.
eg: Use them when traceability is a requirement; asking for reference numbers in prose does not give verifiable spans.

def: A strategy in which an agent keeps lightweight references such as file paths, saved queries or links and loads data into context at run time with tools, instead of pre-loading everything. It is slower than precomputed retrieval but avoids stale indexes and bloat.
eg: Claude Code uses glob and grep this way. A hybrid, where some data is loaded up front, often suits stable content.

def: Loading information in stages as needed: for skills, only the name and description at start, the full instructions when a skill triggers, and bundled files or scripts only when read or run. It keeps the window small however much is installed.
eg: The same idea underlies tool search and just-in-time retrieval, and it is the alternative to a monolithic prompt.

def: Placing all instructions, documents and tool definitions in the prompt up front. It is simple, and fine for small, stable bodies of content, especially when cached, but it spends tokens every turn, accelerates context rot and does not scale.
eg: Decide by size and query pattern: a 90,000-token manual used constantly differs from a 500-page reference needed only in slices.

def: A vendor-neutral standard in which a trace records one request across the system and spans record its steps. Claude's SDKs and API can emit spans for model requests, tool use and Managed Agents sessions to any compatible observability platform.
eg: SDK tracing covers clients using the SDK, while API tracing, configured in the Console, covers any client. Both together give one joined trace.

def: The delay between sending a request and receiving the first generated token. Streaming improves how fast the first token appears, and smaller models and prompt caching shorten it.
eg: A key interactive-latency metric. It is not the same as total generation time.

def: The share of input tokens read from the prompt cache rather than processed fresh, computed from the usage fields on each response. A sudden drop means something is breaking the prefix, and agent loops reading much less than about 80 percent are worth investigating.
eg: Track it per workload. The cache diagnostics feature shows where a prefix diverged.

def: The field on every successful Messages response saying why generation ended: end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, tool_use, pause_turn, refusal or model_context_window_exceeded. Agent loops branch on it, and its distribution reveals truncation and refusals.
eg: Treat max_tokens and refusal as events to handle or alert on, not as normal completions.

def: Handling a response with stop reason refusal by retrying the same request on another model, either with the beta server-side fallbacks parameter or with client-side middleware or your own retry. Server-side fallback is not offered on Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry.
eg: Discard partial output from a refused stream. The fallback credit feature avoids paying the cache cost twice on a client-side retry.

def: Targets agreed before building that say what 'good' means in specific, measurable, achievable and relevant terms, usually across several dimensions at once, such as accuracy on a held-out set, tail latency, cost per task and safety flags.
eg: Anthropic's testing guidance starts here: 'good performance' cannot be evaluated, but 'at least 90 percent correct on 500 held-out cases' can. Even hazy goals such as safety can be quantified.

def: Judging a Claude solution on several criteria together, for example task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy preservation, latency and price, because pushing one score up can quietly damage another.
eg: A prompt that lifts accuracy but doubles latency and cost is not an improvement unless the other targets still hold. Typical exam answer: track guardrail dimensions, not one headline number.

def: The collection of cases, each with an input and a reference answer or grading rule, used to measure a system. It should mirror the real task distribution and include rare, oversized, ambiguous and adversarial inputs, not only tidy examples.
eg: Build it from sampled, anonymized production traffic plus deliberate hard cases. Anthropic's guidance: be task-specific, automate grading where possible, and prefer volume over a few perfect hand-graded cases.

def: A slice of cases never used while writing or tuning prompts, examples or rules, kept aside so the final score shows how the system performs on inputs it was not shaped around.
eg: Without one, scores measure how well the tuning cases were memorized. Refresh it from new traffic over time.

def: Contamination in which evaluation cases or their answers end up inside prompts, few-shot demonstrations or tuning decisions, inflating the score without improving real-world quality.
eg: Classic symptom: near-perfect evaluation, disappointing production. Fix by separating development examples from a held-out set and rebuilding that set from fresh data.

def: Scoring outputs with deterministic rules such as exact match, string match, schema validation or unit tests. It is the fastest, most reliable and cheapest method to scale, but cannot judge nuance such as tone or quality of reasoning.
eg: Use it first wherever the answer is checkable, and add other graders only for what rules cannot capture.

def: Scoring outputs by trained reviewers or domain experts. It is the most flexible and highest-quality judgment, but slow and expensive, so it is used on small samples to calibrate automated graders and settle ambiguous cases.
eg: Anthropic's testing guidance says to avoid it where an automated method will do. Track agreement between reviewers to see whether your criteria are clear.

def: Using a model, guided by a written rubric, to score another model's outputs. It scales to complex judgments that rules cannot capture, but it has to be validated against human labels before it is trusted.
eg: Docs tips: a detailed rubric, a constrained verdict (a label or a 1-5 scale), and letting the grader reason before it scores. A grader working in a fresh context is not swayed by the original run.

def: A written list of explicit, independently checkable criteria that defines what a correct or high-quality output looks like, used by humans or a model grader, ideally with a fixed verdict format such as correct or incorrect.
eg: Vague rubrics ('looks good') give noisy scores; criteria like 'the CSV has a numeric price column' do not. Managed Agents outcomes take a rubric in the same spirit.

def: Checking an automated grader against a sample labeled by people, measuring how often they agree and where they diverge, and adjusting the rubric before relying on the grader at scale.
eg: The docs' advice for model-based grading is to test reliability first, then scale. Low agreement usually means vague criteria, not a grader that is too small.

def: Systematic tilts in model-based grading, such as favoring longer answers, favoring whichever answer is shown first, or rating text that resembles the grader's own style higher. Mitigations are randomized order, criteria that ignore length and checks against human labels.
eg: General evaluation practice rather than a single Claude setting: treat these tilts as risks to test for whenever a model grades.

def: A fixed, versioned set of cases rerun whenever a prompt, model, tool or retrieval setting changes, so that an improvement in one area cannot silently break behavior that used to work.
eg: Every production incident should add its failing case here. Big suites are cheap to run overnight on the Message Batches API; a small fast subset can gate each change.

def: Working in a loop of defining success criteria, building evaluations first, then changing the prompt or design and re-measuring, so every change is justified by its effect on the evaluation rather than by a few hand-picked examples.
eg: Mirrors Anthropic's prompt-engineering cycle: test cases, preliminary prompt, iterate, final validation, ship.

def: The distinction between scoring a system against fixed, labeled cases before release and measuring it on live traffic afterwards through signals such as task completion, user corrections, escalations and feedback.
eg: Offline tells you whether a change is safe to try; online tells you whether it works for real users. Mature programs feed online failures back into the offline set.

def: A controlled experiment that randomly splits concurrent live traffic between a current and a candidate variant of a prompt, model or setting, then compares a pre-chosen primary metric once enough samples have accumulated.
eg: Needs random, sticky assignment, one change at a time, a planned sample size and guardrail metrics. Comparing this week with last week, or stopping when one arm leads, are the usual flawed designs.

def: A measure that must not get worse while an experiment tries to improve the primary metric, for example latency, cost per task, refusal rate on legitimate requests or complaint rate.
eg: A variant that wins on accuracy but breaks a guardrail should not ship as is. Agree guardrails and thresholds before the experiment starts.

def: Running a candidate system on real production inputs alongside the current one, without showing its outputs to users or acting on them, so its behavior can be compared and graded safely.
eg: Good for replacing a rules-based or older-model system: no user risk, real data. It does not reveal how users react to the new outputs.

def: Releasing a change to a small, closely monitored fraction of traffic first and widening exposure in steps only while quality, latency, cost and safety metrics hold, with a ready path back to the previous version.
eg: Unlike shadow mode, canary users do see the new output. Pair it with a feature flag and a rollback plan.

def: Reading a sample of failed cases and sorting them into root-cause categories, such as retrieval miss, ambiguous instruction, wrong tool, truncation or model limit, to decide which fix will remove the most failures.
eg: Do this before changing prompts at random. The largest or most severe category usually deserves the next iteration.

def: Output that is fluent and confident but unsupported by the provided context or by fact, such as an invented citation, figure or policy. Mitigation techniques reduce it but do not eliminate it.
eg: Diagnose the source: missing or stale retrieval, no permission to say 'I don't know', or a task the model cannot do. High-stakes outputs still need verification.

def: The degree to which every claim in an answer is supported by the source material the system supplied, usually checked claim by claim against retrieved passages or quoted evidence.
eg: Measure it separately from fluency or overall correctness. Citations and quote-first prompting make it easier to check.

def: Running the same prompt several times and comparing the results: facts that change from run to run are more likely to be invented, while stable agreement raises (but does not guarantee) confidence.
eg: One of the hallucination checks in Anthropic's guardrail docs. It multiplies cost, so reserve it for high-stakes or sampled checks.

def: Classification metrics: the share of flagged items that were truly positive, the share of all true positives that were found, and the single score (their harmonic mean) that balances both. They matter when classes are rare, where plain accuracy misleads.
eg: A fraud model that labels everything legitimate is 99 percent accurate when fraud is 1 percent of cases, yet useless. Pick the metric that matches the cost of each error type.

def: A retrieval-quality metric: the fraction of labeled questions for which the passage that actually holds the answer appears among the top k results returned, measured independently of what the model then writes.
eg: Track it apart from answer quality so a drop can be traced to the retrieval stage, for example after an index refresh.

def: The fact that the same input can yield different outputs from run to run, so a single run is weak evidence. Evaluations repeat cases, report the spread and constrain what must be stable using structured outputs and validators.
eg: Do not promise bit-identical answers to stakeholders; promise measured tolerances. Newer Claude models accept only the default temperature, so control variance through prompt design and output constraints.

def: The share of adversarial attempts, such as injected documents or jailbreak prompts, that achieve the attacker's goal against the real system with its real tools. It is the main security metric for guardrail and injection testing.
eg: Measure it on a fixed adversarial set, rerun it with every release, and report it next to the false-refusal rate.

def: The share of legitimate, in-policy requests that a system wrongly declines or blocks. It is the cost side of safety controls and must be tracked alongside how many attacks they stop.
eg: A guardrail that drives attack success to zero by blocking 10 percent of real users has not solved the problem. Tune thresholds on both.

def: Grading an agent's path as well as its final answer: which tools it called, in what order, how many steps and tokens it used, and whether it stayed within its permissions.
eg: Two agents can give the same correct answer while one takes three times the tool calls. Track steps, cost per completed task and tool error rate from traces.

def: An asynchronous interface that accepts up to 100,000 requests (or 256 MB) per batch at half the standard token price, with most batches finishing within an hour and a 24-hour maximum. Results are matched to requests by a caller-supplied id, not by order.
eg: Ideal for large evaluation runs and bulk classification when nobody is waiting. Not for streaming, fast mode or interactive work; results stay downloadable for 29 days.

def: Per-model ceilings, enforced per organization and optionally lowered per workspace, on requests per minute and on input and output tokens per minute, replenished continuously like a token bucket. For most models, tokens read from the prompt cache do not count toward the input ceiling.
eg: Exceeding any one returns HTTP 429, often with a retry-after hint; sudden traffic jumps can also trip acceleration limits, so ramp up gradually. Caching raises effective throughput.

def: A retry policy that waits progressively longer after each failure and adds random variation to every wait, so many clients recovering from a 429 or 5xx error do not all retry at the same instant. A server-provided retry-after hint takes precedence.
eg: Official SDKs retry transient errors twice by default with exponential backoff. A monthly spend-cap 429 carries no retry-after and will not clear by retrying.

def: The number of reuses at which the extra cost of writing a prefix to the prompt cache is repaid by cheaper reads. At standard multipliers it is one reuse within the five-minute lifetime and two within the one-hour lifetime.
eg: A prefix reused only once after the short lifetime has expired can cost more with caching than without. Compute it from your own traffic, not on faith.

def: Administrative endpoints that return historical token usage and cost for an organization, groupable by workspace, model or API key. They need an admin-level credential and are the authoritative source for reconciling internal records with the bill.
eg: Use them for chargeback, anomaly alerts and spotting a leaked key; workspace keys do not work for them. Exported traces are best-effort and can miss spans.

def: A per-request record kept for every model call that captures identifiers and measurements rather than free text: model ID, prompt or template version, token usage including cached tokens, stop reason, latency, request id and tool outcomes.
eg: It lets you slice failures by version and release. Avoid storing full prompts and responses by default when they contain personal data.

def: A setting on exported traces that decides whether spans carry only identifiers, timing, status and token counts, or also the full prompts and responses. The identifiers-only choice is the default, and the full choice moves sensitive text into your observability vendor.
eg: Full content helps debug and build evals from real traffic, but the platform stores it under its own retention rules. Organizations with a HIPAA-type restriction export metadata only from API destinations.

def: A gradual, often unnoticed decline in output quality after launch, caused by changing inputs, upstream data or formats, new model versions or stale knowledge. Catching it takes continuous sampling and scheduled re-evaluation, not user complaints alone.
eg: Run the regression suite on a schedule, grade a sample of live traffic, and alert on shifts in stop reasons, refusal rate and validator failures.

def: The set of configurations (model tier, effort, prompt, retrieval depth, caching) for which no alternative is both cheaper and better on your evaluation. Choosing from it means picking the cheapest option that still clears the quality bar.
eg: Plot cost per completed task against pass rate for each candidate; anything below the frontier is dominated and can be dropped.

def: Evidence that a measured difference between two variants is unlikely to be random noise, which depends on sample size, outcome variance and how many comparisons were made. A small lead on a few dozen cases proves little.
eg: Plan the sample size before the experiment, do not stop early just because a variant happens to lead, and report intervals, not only point estimates.

def: Layering several independent safeguards, such as input screening, least-privilege tools, sandboxing, approval gates, output validation and monitoring, so that the failure of any one control does not become a breach.
eg: Anthropic's guardrail guidance chains strategies rather than relying on one. Model behavior is never the only control.

def: A cheap pre-check in which a small, fast model classifies incoming user text (or tool output) as acceptable or harmful, returning a constrained verdict before the main model sees it. If the screening call itself is refused, that counts as a harmful verdict.
eg: Typically Claude Haiku with structured outputs. Run it in parallel to protect latency, and log verdicts to tune thresholds.

def: Checking what the model returned, with schema validation, business-rule checks, classifiers or scans for personal data and leaked secrets, before it reaches users or is passed to downstream systems.
eg: Treat model output as untrusted input to the next system. Programmatic checks hold when prompt wording does not.

def: Attacks in which the user of your application is the adversary and crafts input meant to make the model ignore its guidelines or your instructions. Mitigations include input screening, hardened prompts, throttling repeat offenders and monitoring.
eg: A different threat model from the indirect kind, where the user is trusted but third-party content is hostile.

def: An attack in which the user is trusted but content the model reads on their behalf, such as a web page, email, document or tool result, contains hidden instructions aimed at redirecting the model.
eg: Defend by structure, not hope: untrusted text only inside tool results, labeled with its source and JSON-encoded, with least-privilege tools and approvals for risky actions.

def: The rule, stated in the system prompt and reinforced by how data is delivered, that text from tools, documents and searches is data to report on and never a source of instructions that can change goals or trigger tools the user did not request.
eg: Part of Anthropic's recommended hardening. Your own instructions belong in the system prompt, or in a user turn after the tool result, not inside it.

def: Exposure of confidential material placed in a system prompt, such as proprietary formulas or internal rules, when the model is coaxed into repeating it. Instructions to keep it secret are not a dependable defense: keep secrets out of prompts and screen outputs.
eg: Anthropic suggests monitoring first (output screening), using leak-resistance only when necessary because it can hurt task performance, and omitting unneeded proprietary detail.

def: The maximum damage a compromised, mistaken or manipulated agent action can cause, determined by the tools, credentials, data, network reach and autonomy it holds. Shrinking it is the main way to make a successful attack survivable.
eg: Reduce it with least-privilege tool sets, scoped credentials in vaults, sandboxing, network limits and approvals sized to impact.

def: Running agent-executed code and shell commands inside an isolated environment with restricted filesystem access and a network allowlist enforced by the operating system or container, so even approved or injected commands cannot reach arbitrary files or hosts.
eg: Permission rules alone are not enough: denying a fetch tool does not stop curl through an allowed shell. A domain allowlist enforced at the OS level closes that gap.

def: Choosing, for a safety or policy control that becomes unavailable or errors out, to deny the action or refuse to start rather than proceed unchecked. It trades some availability for assurance.
eg: Appears as the block-or-allow failure setting of inference hooks and as fail-closed startup for Claude Code managed settings. Choose it for high-risk flows.

def: Abuse or runaway behavior that drives up spend rather than breaking availability, such as a public endpoint hammered with long requests or an agent looping on a failing tool. Defenses are authentication, per-user quotas, budgets and caps, and alerts.
eg: Combine application limits with workspace spend and rate limits so one workload cannot exhaust the organization's quota.

def: The exposure created by third-party skills, plugins and MCP servers, which can carry scripts, hidden instructions or network calls that exfiltrate data. Treat installing them like deploying software: review contents, sandbox, pin versions and keep a registry.
eg: Anthropic's enterprise skills guidance gives a review checklist and says authors should not review their own work.

def: A structured description of what is being protected, who might attack or misuse it, through which entry points, and which controls address each path. For an LLM system the paths include user input, retrieved content, tool results and the model's own actions.
eg: Produce it during design with security staff, and revisit it when tools or data sources change.

def: A maintained list of identified risks, each with a description, likelihood and impact, an accountable owner, planned mitigations and the residual risk after them, reviewed on a schedule.
eg: Typical LLM entries: hallucination in a high-stakes answer, injection through retrieved content, model retirement, cost overrun, bias. General delivery practice rather than a Claude feature.

def: Deliberate adversarial testing of a system before and after launch, using hostile documents, emails, tool outputs and user prompts against the real tool configuration, to find failures and measure how often attacks succeed.
eg: Rerun a fixed attack set on every release so fixes do not regress.

def: Designing a workflow so a person reviews, approves or can override model output before a consequential action or delivery, with the reviewer placed where error cost and irreversibility are highest rather than at every step.
eg: Variants: approve before acting, review a sample after acting, escalate only exceptions. Reviewers must have the authority and time to change the outcome.

def: A rule that routes a case from automation to a person, preferably based on checkable signals such as a failed validator, a high monetary amount, a policy flag or weak retrieval support rather than the model's own claim of confidence.
eg: Self-reported confidence should be treated as unvalidated until it has been measured against ground truth.

def: Having people check a random, and risk-weighted, sample of outputs that were released automatically, to estimate the true error rate, catch drift and justify when full review is unnecessary.
eg: Gives a measured, defensible basis for loosening or tightening oversight over time.

def: The tendency of reviewers to over-trust machine output and approve it with little scrutiny, especially when it is usually right. Rubber-stamping defeats the purpose of human review.
eg: Counter it with seeded known-bad items, evidence shown beside each recommendation, and tracking of reviewer overrides and time per item.

def: Conditions in Anthropic's Usage Policy for uses that affect a person's health, legal rights, finances, employment, housing, education or access to services: a qualified person must meaningfully review the AI recommendation, and the affected individual must be told AI was involved.
eg: Treat these as design requirements, not paperwork. Check the current policy text and local law for the exact scope.

def: A control that keeps the person who creates or changes something, such as a prompt, skill or policy, from being the only one who approves it, so one mistake or bad actor cannot ship unchecked.
eg: Anthropic's enterprise skills guidance requires that skill authors not be their own reviewers.

def: A tamper-resistant record of who or what did what, when, with which inputs, versions and approvals, kept long enough to reconstruct and justify a decision after the fact.
eg: For LLM systems include prompt and model versions, tool calls, human approvals and the sources used.

def: Sending the model, and storing afterwards, only the personal or sensitive fields the task needs, for example by selecting columns, redacting identifiers or replacing them with pseudonyms before the call and restoring them afterwards.
eg: Supports GDPR-style principles and the HIPAA minimum-necessary idea, and it shrinks the blast radius of any leak.

def: A contractual arrangement, enabled per organization by Anthropic, under which customer prompts and responses are not stored at rest after the API response is returned. Stateful features such as batch jobs and stored files fall outside it.
eg: Flagged content and legal holds can still be retained, and the Covered Models require 30-day retention. Always check the feature eligibility table.

def: An API arrangement for organizations handling protected health information: a signed business associate agreement plus organization-wide safeguards, with the API rejecting requests that use features outside coverage. It is organization-level and cannot be turned off once enabled.
eg: An alternative to ZDR for PHI, not an add-on. Keep PHI out of JSON schema definitions, and use a separate organization for non-HIPAA work.

def: The designation for Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, which require 30-day data retention and so are unavailable under zero data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it. Requests from a non-qualifying organization or workspace fail with a 400 error.
eg: A ZDR organization can enable 30-day retention on one non-default workspace to use them there.

def: Two independent data-residency settings on the first-party API: a per-request (or workspace-default) choice of where inference runs, currently global or the US, and a workspace-creation choice of where data is stored at rest, currently only the US.
eg: US-only inference costs 1.1 times the standard token price on Claude 4.6 and later models. For EU-only processing, use a partner-platform regional endpoint instead.

def: The two GDPR roles: the party that decides why and how personal data is processed, and the party that processes it on that party's behalf under a written agreement. Which role a vendor holds shapes contracts and due diligence.
eg: On the first-party Claude API Anthropic is the data processor; on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud's Agent Platform the cloud provider is.

def: A US federal program that standardizes security assessment, authorization and continuous monitoring of cloud services used by government agencies, at Low, Moderate and High impact baselines. Workloads that need it must run on services holding the right level.
eg: Anthropic's docs point organizations that require the High baseline to Claude in Amazon Bedrock, where AWS operates the service.

def: Individual rights under the EU's data-protection regulation, including access to data, correction, erasure and safeguards around solely automated decisions, which an LLM pipeline can honor only if it knows where personal data is stored and can find and delete it.
eg: Design for deletion up front: limit what is stored, set retention periods, and keep personal data out of long-lived indexes and logs. General compliance practice; confirm specifics with counsel.

def: An opt-in arrangement in which you hold the key that encrypts your workspace data at rest in your own cloud key service (AWS, Google Cloud or Azure), keeping control of rotation, audit and revocation. Anthropic keeps no copy, so losing the key destroys the data.
eg: It protects data written after the key takes effect, so attach it to a new workspace before traffic. Enabling it is permanent.

def: An audit capability, available to eligible customers on request, that records each human view of covered customer content by Anthropic personnel, permitted only under published reason codes, as events in the organization's compliance activity feed.
eg: Automated safety processing does not generate events. Pair it with the Compliance API for the audit trail.

def: Programmatic, after-the-fact access for security, legal and compliance teams to an organization's activity feed and, for Claude Enterprise, to users, roles, chats, files, projects and session transcripts, using a dedicated access key.
eg: It retrieves records; it does not block requests. Inline blocking is the job of inference hooks.

def: A beta capability for Claude Enterprise organizations that sends each governed prompt to the organization's own security server and waits for an allow or deny verdict before inference runs. Failures follow a configured block-or-allow setting, and a shadow mode lets teams observe without blocking.
eg: Verdicts are allow or deny only (no rewriting). Not available to Console API organizations, Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud.

def: Measuring quality, error rates and refusal rates separately for subgroups, such as demographic groups, languages or customer segments, including counterfactual pairs that differ only in a protected attribute, to expose unequal performance that an overall average hides.
eg: Removing names or other attributes from inputs is not enough, because proxies can remain. Fairness findings need owners and fixes, not just charts.

def: Telling users and affected individuals clearly that they are interacting with, or being assessed with the help of, an AI system, along with its limits and how to reach a human. It supports trust and, for high-risk decisions, is required by policy and often by law.
eg: It does not have to name the vendor or model. Pair it with citations and an appeal path.

def: A deliberate early phase that gathers the business problem, current workflow and volumes, decision owners and users, data sources and sensitivity, error costs, constraints and success measures through interviews, process mapping and data review before any architecture is chosen.
eg: Outputs: a problem statement, baseline numbers, constraints and acceptance criteria. Jumping to model choice first is the usual failure.

def: Measurements of how the current process performs today, such as handling time, error and rework rates, cost per case and volume, captured before building so that improvement and return on investment can be demonstrated rather than asserted.
eg: Without a baseline, 'it feels faster' is the only evidence a sponsor gets.

def: The qualities a solution must have beyond its features, such as accuracy thresholds, latency, availability, throughput, cost ceilings, security, data residency, auditability and explainability. For Claude systems they drive model tier, caching, deployment platform and oversight design.
eg: Elicit them explicitly; stakeholders rarely volunteer 'p95 under 3 seconds' or 'EU-only processing'.

def: Testable conditions, agreed with the sponsor before the build, that decide whether the solution is accepted, ideally expressed as thresholds on an evaluation set, for example at least 95 percent correct on representative cases with no critical-severity errors.
eg: They turn arguments about quality into measurements, and the evaluation suite becomes the acceptance test.

def: A living list of what the team is taking for granted (data quality, user behavior, API limits, vendor roadmap) and what is fixed (budget, deadline, regulation, platform), each with an owner and a way to check it, so surprises surface early.
eg: Revisit it when a model is deprecated or rate limits change; both invalidate common assumptions.

def: A table assigning each activity or decision to who is Responsible for doing it, who is Accountable for the outcome, who must be Consulted and who is only Informed. It prevents gaps such as legal reviewing too late.
eg: Name security, legal, compliance and operations during discovery; finding a veto holder late is expensive.

def: A schedule of who receives which information, how often and in what form, such as executive summaries, demos, metric reports and incident notices, matched to each audience's concerns.
eg: Executives want value and risk, security wants controls and data flow, operations want runbooks and service objectives: same facts, different views.

def: The full cost of running a solution over its life: model usage, retrieval and infrastructure, integration and engineering, evaluation, human review time, monitoring and support, training and change management, not just the token bill.
eg: Token spend is often a minority of the total in high-oversight workflows.

def: The ratio of measured benefits to total cost, built from baseline numbers, pilot results (automation rate, error and rework changes) and a complete cost model, shown with ranges and stated assumptions rather than a single optimistic figure.
eg: A defensible business case uses cost per completed task and a sensitivity analysis.

def: A short, dated document capturing one significant design decision: the context, options considered, criteria, the choice made, its consequences and when to revisit it, kept alongside the design so the reasoning survives staff changes.
eg: Handy for 'why this model tier?' questions months later, when a newer model ships.

def: A table that scores candidate options against weighted criteria such as accuracy, latency, cost, security and effort, making trade-offs explicit and discussable instead of argued from preference.
eg: Agree the weights with stakeholders before scoring, and check whether the winner changes when the weights move.

def: A small, time-boxed build that tests whether the core idea is feasible and valuable on real data, aimed at answering a few risky questions rather than at production quality.
eg: Do not ship it as is: it typically lacks evaluation depth, security review, monitoring and support.

def: A limited live trial with real users and real workflows, often with extra human oversight, used to measure outcomes against acceptance criteria and gather feedback before wider rollout.
eg: Choose representative users; a friendly team makes results look better than they will be at scale.

def: A formal checkpoint between lifecycle phases, such as discovery to design or pilot to production, where agreed criteria (evaluation results, security review, operational readiness, budget) must be met before work proceeds.
eg: Gates make go or no-go a measurement, not a mood.

def: A contractual commitment to a customer on measurable service levels, such as availability and response time, with defined consequences if missed. It should promise only what the architecture and its dependencies can sustain.
eg: Do not promise more than your least reliable dependency without fallbacks and graceful degradation.

def: An internal target for a measured service level, for example 99 percent of answers within 5 seconds, usually set tighter than the external commitment, tracked through indicators and used to decide when reliability work takes priority.
eg: For LLM systems add quality objectives (accuracy on sampled traffic) beside latency and availability.

def: The amount of unreliability a service may incur within an objective over a period, for example 1 percent of requests. The remaining amount guides whether to ship risky changes or pause for stability work.
eg: Gives product and engineering one shared number instead of an argument.

def: A paid service tier that gave requests priority over standard traffic, with fewer overload errors, under committed capacity. New capacity commitments are no longer sold, although existing ones run to the end of their contract.
eg: Do not build an availability promise on buying it; design for retries, fallbacks and headroom. The standard tier is best-effort.

def: Designing a system to keep serving a reduced but acceptable experience when a dependency fails or is slow, for example showing search results without a generated summary, serving a cached answer, queuing for later or handing off to a person.
eg: Plan it per dependency, test it, and tell users clearly when they are in degraded mode.

def: Estimating peak demand in requests and tokens and comparing it with rate limits, quotas and budgets well before launch, then requesting higher limits, smoothing load, caching and ramping traffic gradually.
eg: Tier increases take time, and sudden traffic jumps can trip acceleration limits.

def: The people side of a rollout: engaging affected users early, training them, setting honest expectations about what the AI can and cannot do, naming champions, providing a feedback channel and phasing adoption.
eg: Technical success with unprepared users still fails. Claude Code's champion and communications kits are examples.
